_comment: Mutations for the two background-loop bodies. Scored against loops_run.sh, the probe pair — no HTTP harness can reach either one. This spec matters more than most: the plan names these loops as "the least testable part and the most likely to silently diverge, because nothing calls them and nothing returns", and the Python's own history bears that out — an AttributeError in the cleanup ran nightly, swallowed by the loop's try/except, until a Sentry alert surfaced it. Several mutations here change a COUNT and nothing else, or the rows and not the count; the probe prints both for that reason.

mutations.name: a node never heard from is announced as offline
mutations._why: `last_seen IS NOT NULL` is the filter that keeps a row which has never reported from being announced as having gone offline. Drop it and every freshly created node gets a spurious 'went offline' the first time the sweep runs — before its first heartbeat, which is exactly the window an operator is watching.
mutations.old:
"UPDATE camera_nodes SET status = 'offline'
          WHERE status = 'online' AND last_seen IS NOT NULL AND last_seen < $1
mutations.new:
"UPDATE camera_nodes SET status = 'offline'
          WHERE status = 'online' AND last_seen < $1
mutations.equivalent: Equivalent, and verified rather than assumed: `NULL < timestamp` evaluates to NULL and `WHERE` treats that as not-true, so the comparison ALONE already excludes a row that has never reported. Checked against the fixture — 2 rows matched with the predicate and 2 without. SQLAlchemy emits the same SQL, so it is equally redundant in the Python. The predicate stays in both because it states the intent, and this entry stays so the next reader does not take its presence for evidence that it is load-bearing.

mutations.name: a camera never heard from is announced as offline
mutations._why: The same filter on the camera half. Separate mutation because it is a separate statement and a port can easily carry one and not the other.
mutations.old: WHERE c.status = 'online' AND c.last_seen IS NOT NULL AND c.last_seen < $1
mutations.equivalent: Equivalent, and verified rather than assumed: `NULL < timestamp` evaluates to NULL and `WHERE` treats that as not-true, so the comparison ALONE already excludes a row that has never reported. Checked against the fixture — 2 rows matched with the predicate and 2 without. SQLAlchemy emits the same SQL, so it is equally redundant in the Python. The predicate stays in both because it states the intent, and this entry stays so the next reader does not take its presence for evidence that it is load-bearing.

mutations.name: an already-offline node is announced again
mutations._why: `status = 'online'` is what makes the sweep a TRANSITION and not a state assertion. Without it every stale row is re-announced on every tick — one notification per node every thirty seconds, forever.
mutations.old: WHERE status = 'online' AND last_seen IS NOT NULL AND last_seen < $1
mutations.new: WHERE last_seen IS NOT NULL AND last_seen < $1

mutations.name: the heartbeat threshold is ten times too long
mutations._why: 90 seconds, and it has to be the same 90 `effective_status` uses — at 900 a camera reads offline in the dashboard for a quarter of an hour while the sweep still thinks it is online, so no notification ever fires for it.

mutations.name: a nameless node is announced with an empty title
mutations._why: `name or node_id` — a node whose name is blank is announced by its id, because a notification reading "Node '' went offline" tells an operator nothing about which box to go and look at.

mutations.name: a camera's transition loses its parent node
mutations._why: The notification's `node_id` is how the dashboard groups a camera's alert under the box that hosts it. Resolved through the FK rather than assumed, because a camera may have no node at all.
mutations.old: (SELECT n.node_id FROM camera_nodes n WHERE n.id = c.node_id) AS parent",

mutations.name: cameras are announced before nodes
mutations._why: Nodes first, then cameras — the notification ids follow the emit order and a client renders the inbox by id, so an operator sees the uplink drop before the cameras behind it rather than after. Invisible to a snapshot that sorts by anything but id, which is why the probe carries a row_number.

mutations.name: every org gets the same retention
mutations._why: Retention is the tier's, not a constant: Free 30 days, Pro 90, Pro Plus 365. A fixed 90 silently deletes eleven months of a Pro Plus org's audit trail and keeps two months of a free one's.

mutations.name: notifications are swept on the wrong column
mutations._why: `notifications` is the one log table whose timestamp is `created_at`; three others use `timestamp` and the stream log uses `accessed_at`. They are not interchangeable — and a wrong guess here does not error, it deletes nothing and reports zero, which reads exactly like a clean sweep.
mutations.old: "DELETE FROM notifications WHERE org_id = $1 AND created_at < $2",
mutations.new: "DELETE FROM notifications WHERE org_id = $1 AND created_at < $2 AND false",

mutations.name: a pending email is deleted with the old sent ones
mutations._why: The outbox sweep is terminal-state only. A pending or sending row is an email that has NOT gone out yet, and deleting one loses it with nothing left to show it existed — the fixture carries a 400-day pending row for exactly this.

mutations.name: the outbox window follows the tier
mutations._why: Seven days, fixed and cross-org. The outbox is a queue the worker scans every tick, so it wants to be small at all times; the long-term per-org trail is email_log's job. A 365-day window on a Pro Plus org makes the hot scan target a year deep.

mutations.name: webhook markers are swept inside Svix's retry window
mutations._why: 30 days, chosen to comfortably exceed Svix's ~5-day retry window. Sweep at 3 and a retried delivery finds no marker and double-processes — which for a subscription webhook means re-applying a plan change, and for Resend means re-suppressing an address.

mutations.name: an org with only email activity is skipped
mutations._why: `email_log` is in the UNION so an org whose only rows are emails still has its retention applied. Without it that org's log grows forever, and it is the least likely to be noticed because nothing else about the org looks active.

mutations.name: an empty org_id is swept as an org
mutations._why: Python filters on `if row[0]`, which is false for an empty string as well as NULL. An empty org_id is a corrupt row; resolving a plan for it means a Clerk lookup for an org that does not exist, and counting it inflates orgs_processed.

mutations.name: the org list counts duplicates
mutations._why: UNION, not UNION ALL: an org with rows in all six tables appears six times under ALL, which sweeps it six times (harmless, the second is a no-op) and reports orgs_processed six times too high — the one number an operator uses to sanity-check the sweep. EVERY union has to change: the first version of this mutation changed only the first, and `A UNION ALL B UNION C` still dedupes the whole accumulated result at the later UNION, so the mutant was equivalent by construction.
mutations.old:
"SELECT org_id FROM stream_access_logs
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM mcp_activity_logs
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM audit_log
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM motion_events
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM notifications
         UNION SELECT org_id FROM email_log",
mutations.new:
"SELECT org_id FROM stream_access_logs
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM mcp_activity_logs
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM audit_log
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM motion_events
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM notifications
         UNION ALL SELECT org_id FROM email_log",

mutations.name: the cutoff is inclusive
mutations._why: `<`, not `<=`. Not about the single row that lands exactly on the boundary so much as the shape: a retention window stated as "90 days" should keep the row at exactly 90 days old. Scored against the probe's whole-day ages, where a row sits on the boundary by construction.
mutations.old: "DELETE FROM stream_access_logs WHERE org_id = $1 AND accessed_at < $2",
mutations.new: "DELETE FROM stream_access_logs WHERE org_id = $1 AND accessed_at <= $2",
mutations.equivalent: A row exactly on the cutoff to the microsecond cannot be arranged from a fixture written in whole days — the ages are relative to now() and every row is milliseconds off the boundary. Kept in the spec as a record of the comparison being deliberate; the boundary itself is pinned by the fixture's 45-and-200-day rows sitting either side of each tier.

mutations.name: the summary under-reports the sweep
mutations._why: The total is what the log line shows an operator. Leaving a table out of the sum under-reports a nightly sweep that deleted hundreds of thousands of rows, and there is nothing else to notice it by.
